title: Imports and Setup
content: The formalization imports Mathlib's SimpleGraph module for graph-theoretic structures, Cardinal for infinite cardinal arithmetic, and basic set operations. The `open Cardinal SimpleGraph` command brings cardinal and graph notations into scope, and the `Erdos740` namespace isolates the formalization.
mathContext: We work with `SimpleGraph V` (symmetric irreflexive relations on vertex type $V$) and `Cardinal` (the type of cardinals in ZFC set theory, including transfinite cardinals like $\aleph_0, \aleph_1, \ldots$).

title: Chromatic Number
content: The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the minimum number of colors needed to properly color a graph $G$, where adjacent vertices receive different colors. For infinite graphs, this is a cardinal number rather than a natural number, allowing us to discuss graphs with $\chi(G) = \aleph_0$ or larger infinite cardinals.
mathContext: For a graph $G = (V, E)$, we define $\chi(G) = \min\{\kappa : G \text{ is } \kappa\text{-colorable}\}$ where $\kappa$ ranges over cardinals. When $V$ is infinite, $\chi(G)$ can be any cardinal $\leq |V|$.

title: k-Colorable
content: A graph is $k$-colorable if there exists a function $f : V \to k$ assigning colors to vertices such that adjacent vertices receive different colors. This is the standard proper coloring condition extended to arbitrary cardinals.
mathContext: $G$ is $\kappa$-colorable iff $\exists f: V \to \kappa$ such that $\forall v, w \in V$, $G.\text{Adj}(v, w) \implies f(v) \neq f(w)$.

title: Cycle Structure
content: A cycle of length $n$ is formalized as a structure with $n$ distinct vertices forming a closed walk where consecutive vertices are adjacent. The fields enforce: (1) closure (first vertex equals last), (2) adjacency along the path, and (3) distinctness of internal vertices.
mathContext: A cycle $C_n$ in graph $G$ is a sequence $(v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{n-1})$ with $v_0 = v_{n-1}$, each $v_i v_{i+1} \in E(G)$, and all $v_i$ distinct (except $v_0 = v_{n-1}$).

title: Odd Cycle
content: A cycle is odd if its length $n$ is odd (3, 5, 7, ...). Odd cycles are fundamental to graph theory: by a classical result, a graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd cycles. The smallest odd cycle is the triangle ($C_3$).
mathContext: A cycle $C_n$ is odd iff $n \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$. By K\"onig's theorem, $G$ is bipartite $\iff$ $G$ contains no odd cycle.

title: Triangle
content: A triangle ($C_3$) is the smallest possible cycle and the smallest odd cycle. Triangle-free graphs form a central class in extremal graph theory, studied extensively since Mantel's theorem (1907) and the Ramsey-theoretic results of Erdos.
mathContext: The triangle $C_3 = K_3$ is both the smallest cycle and the complete graph on 3 vertices. Mantel's theorem: $\text{ex}(n, K_3) = \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$.

title: Contains Short Odd Cycle
content: The predicate `containsOddCycleLeq V G r` asserts that $G$ contains at least one odd cycle of length at most $r$. This existential statement is the negation of the cycle-avoidance property central to Problem #740.
mathContext: $\text{containsOddCycleLeq}(G, r) :\iff \exists n \leq r,\; n \text{ odd},\; C_n \subseteq G$.

title: No Short Odd Cycles
content: The key property for Problem #740: a graph avoids all odd cycles of length $\leq r$. When $r = 3$, this means triangle-free. This property must be preserved in the subgraph while maintaining the same chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$.
mathContext: $\text{noOddCyclesLeq}(G, r) :\iff \neg\exists n \leq r,\; n \text{ odd},\; C_n \subseteq G$. Equivalently, the odd girth of $G$ exceeds $r$.

title: Triangle-Free
content: A graph is triangle-free iff it has no odd cycles of length $\leq 3$, which is equivalent to having no 3-cycles at all (since 1 and 2 are not valid cycle lengths). This is the most studied special case of cycle avoidance, central to Rodl's resolution of the countable case.
mathContext: $\text{isTriangleFree}(G) :\iff \text{noOddCyclesLeq}(G, 3)$. By Ramsey theory, $R(3,k) = \Theta(k^2/\log k)$, so triangle-free graphs can still have large chromatic number.

title: Induced Subgraph
content: The induced subgraph $G[S]$ on vertex subset $S \subseteq V$ retains exactly those edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $S$. This is the natural restriction operation and the type of subgraph used in the Erdos-Hajnal conjecture.
mathContext: For $S \subseteq V(G)$, $G[S] = (S, \{uv \in E(G) : u, v \in S\})$. Note $\chi(G[S]) \leq \chi(G)$ always holds.

title: Has Subgraph With Property
content: The key existential predicate: $G$ has a subgraph satisfying property $P$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$. This packages the two requirements of Problem #740 (preserving chromatic number AND satisfying a cycle-avoidance condition) into a single predicate.
mathContext: $\text{hasSubgraphWith}(G, \mathfrak{m}, P) :\iff \exists S \subseteq V,\; P(G[S]) \wedge \chi(G[S]) = \mathfrak{m}$.

title: The Erdos-Hajnal Conjecture (Problem #740)
content:
The central conjecture: if $\chi(G) = \mathfrak{m}$ is an infinite cardinal, then $G$ must contain an induced subgraph with the same chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ that avoids all odd cycles of length $\leq r$. This asserts that high chromatic number forces rich substructure even under cycle restrictions.

This was formulated by Erdos and Hajnal and appears in Erdos's 1981 paper [Er81] as one of the problems he 'would most like to see solved.'
mathContext: For infinite $\mathfrak{m}$ and $r \geq 1$: $\chi(G) = \mathfrak{m} \implies \exists S \subseteq V,\; \chi(G[S]) = \mathfrak{m} \wedge \text{oddGirth}(G[S]) > r$.

title: Triangle-Free Conjecture
content: The special case $r = 3$: must every graph with infinite chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ contain a triangle-free subgraph with $\chi = \mathfrak{m}$? This is the most studied and best-understood case, resolved by Rodl for countable chromatic number.
mathContext: $\text{triangleFreeConjecture}(\mathfrak{m}) :\iff \text{erdosHajnalConjecture}(\mathfrak{m}, 3)$.

title: Countable Case
content: The conjecture specialized to $\mathfrak{m} = \aleph_0$: every graph with countably infinite chromatic number must contain a subgraph with the same chromatic number and no odd cycles of length $\leq r$. This is the case Rodl resolved for $r = 3$ using a sophisticated probabilistic argument.
mathContext: $\text{countableCase}(r) :\iff \forall G,\; \chi(G) = \aleph_0 \implies \exists S,\; \chi(G[S]) = \aleph_0 \wedge \text{noOddCyclesLeq}(G[S], r)$.

title: Rodl's Theorem
content:
Rodl's theorem (1977): every graph with $\chi = \aleph_0$ contains a triangle-free subgraph with $\chi = \aleph_0$. This is the deepest result formalized here, stated as an axiom since the proof uses advanced probabilistic methods beyond current Mathlib formalization capabilities.

Rodl's proof introduced the technique of random vertex selection with careful probability estimates, which became influential in combinatorics.
mathContext: Rodl proved $\text{countableCase}(3)$: $\chi(G) = \aleph_0 \implies \exists H \subseteq G,\; \chi(H) = \aleph_0 \wedge K_3 \not\subseteq H$. The proof uses the probabilistic method in infinite combinatorics.

title: Countable Triangle-Free Corollary
content: A direct corollary restating Rodl's theorem: the countable case with $r = 3$ is resolved. This trivial deduction from the axiom demonstrates the formalization's structure.
mathContext: $\text{countable\_triangle\_free} = \text{rodl\_theorem} : \text{countableCase}(3)$.

title: Threshold Function $f_r(\mathfrak{m})$
content: A quantitative refinement: does there exist a cardinal $f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ such that $\chi(G) \geq f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ guarantees a subgraph with $\chi = \mathfrak{m}$ avoiding odd cycles $\leq r$? This asks not just whether the phenomenon occurs, but how much chromatic surplus is needed.
mathContext: $\text{thresholdFunctionExists}(\mathfrak{m}, r) :\iff \exists f,\; \chi(G) \geq f \implies \exists H \subseteq G,\; \chi(H) = \mathfrak{m} \wedge \text{noOddCyclesLeq}(H, r)$.

title: Threshold Function Open
content: The existence of the threshold function $f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ remains unknown for most combinations of $r$ and $\mathfrak{m}$. Even determining whether such a function is well-defined is a major open problem.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of threshold function open

title: Girth
content: The girth of a graph $G$ is the length of its shortest cycle, or $\infty$ if $G$ is acyclic (a forest). Graphs with high girth are sparse yet can still have arbitrarily large chromatic number, as shown by Erdos's 1959 probabilistic existence proof.
mathContext: $\text{girth}(G) = \min\{|C| : C \text{ is a cycle in } G\}$, with $\text{girth}(G) = \infty$ if $G$ is a forest. Erdos (1959) proved: $\forall g, k,\; \exists G$ with $\text{girth}(G) > g$ and $\chi(G) > k$.

title: Girth Greater Than r
content: The predicate asserting that $G$ has no cycles of any length $\leq r$ (equivalently, $\text{girth}(G) > r$). This is strictly stronger than forbidding only odd cycles $\leq r$, since it also eliminates even cycles.
mathContext: $\text{girthGreaterThan}(G, r) :\iff \forall n \leq r,\; C_n \not\subseteq G \iff \text{girth}(G) > r$.

title: Girth Variant Conjecture
content: A stronger variant of Problem #740: must $G$ with $\chi = \mathfrak{m}$ contain a subgraph with $\chi = \mathfrak{m}$ and girth $> r$? This forbids ALL short cycles (not just odd ones), making it strictly harder to satisfy. If true, it would immediately imply the odd cycle version.
mathContext: $\text{girthConjecture}(\mathfrak{m}, r) :\iff \chi(G) = \mathfrak{m} \implies \exists H \subseteq G,\; \chi(H) = \mathfrak{m} \wedge \text{girth}(H) > r$.

title: Girth Implies Odd Cycle Avoidance
content: A formally verified implication: the girth conjecture implies the Erdos-Hajnal conjecture for the same parameters. The proof is straightforward: if a subgraph has no cycles of any length $\leq r$, it certainly has no odd cycles of length $\leq r$. This is one of the few fully proved results in the formalization.
mathContext: $\text{girthConjecture}(\mathfrak{m}, r) \implies \text{erdosHajnalConjecture}(\mathfrak{m}, r)$. Proof: $\text{girth}(H) > r \implies \text{oddGirth}(H) > r$.

title: Finite Analog
content: The finite version of Problem #740: given a finite graph with $\chi(G) \geq n$, can we find a subgraph with $\chi \geq k$ and no odd cycles of length $\leq r$? This connects to the Erdos-Nesetril conjecture and results in finite extremal graph theory.
mathContext: $\text{finiteAnalog}(n, k, r) :\iff \forall G \text{ finite},\; \chi(G) \geq n \implies \exists H \subseteq G,\; \chi(H) \geq k \wedge \text{noOddCyclesLeq}(H, r)$.

title: Finite Triangle-Free Progress
content: An axiom asserting partial progress on the finite $r = 3$ case: there exists a constant $c$ such that every graph with $\chi \geq c$ contains a triangle-free subgraph with $\chi \geq 3$. This is inspired by results of Thomassen and others on forcing triangle-free subgraphs with high chromatic number.
mathContext: $\exists c \in \mathbb{N},\; \text{finiteAnalog}(c, 3, 3)$. Related to Thomassen's result that $\chi(G) \geq 4$ implies $G$ has a triangle-free subgraph with $\chi \geq 3$.

title: Bipartite Graph
content: A graph is bipartite iff it contains no odd cycles of any length. Equivalently, it is 2-colorable: $\chi(G) \leq 2$. This classical characterization (Konig's theorem) is crucial for understanding the limitations of Problem #740.
mathContext: $\text{isBipartite}(G) \iff \forall n \text{ odd},\; C_n \not\subseteq G \iff \chi(G) \leq 2$.

title: No Infinite Bipartite Subgraph
content: For $\mathfrak{m} > 2$, it is impossible to find a bipartite subgraph with $\chi = \mathfrak{m}$, because every bipartite graph has $\chi \leq 2$. This shows that Problem #740 must have a finite bound $r$: the 'avoid ALL odd cycles' (bipartite) version fails for large chromatic numbers. The proof uses sorry for the final contradiction step.
mathContext: $\mathfrak{m} > 2 \implies \neg(\forall G,\; \chi(G) = \mathfrak{m} \implies \exists H \subseteq G,\; \chi(H) = \mathfrak{m} \wedge H \text{ bipartite})$, since bipartite $\implies \chi \leq 2 < \mathfrak{m}$.

title: Summary Theorem
content: Combines the three main results into a single conjunction: (1) Rodl's theorem resolving the countable triangle-free case, (2) the girth conjecture implying the odd cycle conjecture, and (3) the impossibility of bipartite subgraphs with $\chi > 2$. This provides a complete picture of what is currently known about Problem #740.
mathContext: $\text{erdos\_740\_summary} : \text{countableCase}(3) \wedge (\text{girthConj} \Rightarrow \text{oddCycleConj}) \wedge (\mathfrak{m} > 2 \implies \neg\text{bipartiteVersion})$.

title: Main Theorem (Erdos 740)
content: The main exported theorem: $\text{countableCase}(3)$, i.e., Rodl's theorem. This identifies the strongest known positive result as the headline theorem of the formalization.
mathContext: $\text{erdos\_740} : \text{countableCase}(3) = \text{rodl\_theorem}$.

title: Open Question
content: The formalization records the open question explicitly: does the Erdos-Hajnal conjecture hold for all infinite cardinals $\mathfrak{m}$ and all $r \geq 1$? This remains one of the major unsolved problems in infinite graph theory.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of open question

title: Erdos's Most Wanted Problem
content: The full universally quantified conjecture: for ALL infinite cardinals $\mathfrak{m}$ and ALL $r \geq 1$, the conjecture holds. Erdos listed this in his 1981 paper 'On the combinatorial problems which I would most like to see solved' ([Er81]), placing it among approximately 50 problems he considered most important. The problem also appears in his 1995 survey [Er95d].
mathContext: $\text{erdosMostWanted} :\iff \forall \mathfrak{m} \text{ infinite},\; \forall r \geq 1,\; \text{erdosHajnalConjecture}(\mathfrak{m}, r)$.
